groups.stem: Good X costs $3 and good Y costs $6. What is the opportunity cost of one unit of X in units of Y?
Labor-market case B: Two otherwise similar jobs pay differently because one exposes workers to substantial danger. What can explain the pay gap?
Labor-market case D: One household receives a large inheritance while another with similar current earnings does not. What source of wealth inequality is most direct?
A study of hypothetical Economy C reports that the official threshold for a household is $26,000 and measured money income is $27,800. Under that rule, how is the household classified?
Transfer-program case B: Medicaid pays participating providers for covered medical services. What makes this assistance in kind?
keys: Recipients receive specified health-care coverage rather than unrestricted cash

groups.stem: Transfer-program case D: Why might a recipient prefer an equal-value cash transfer to a restricted food benefit?
keys: Cash permits spending on the recipient's highest-priority need

groups.stem: Redistribution proposal B: Which redistribution principle places the greatest weight on improving the position of the least advantaged?
Redistribution proposal D: Why might a libertarian object to redistribution even if it narrows measured inequality?
keys: The policy may violate rights to legitimately acquired income or property

groups.stem: Antipoverty design A: A benefit falls by $0.60 for each additional dollar a recipient earns. What policy-design concern arises?
keys: The phaseout reduces the net reward from working more

groups.stem: Antipoverty design C: How can a gradual benefit phaseout reduce a benefits cliff?
keys: It spreads benefit reductions across a wider earnings range

groups.stem: Suppose that sellers know product quality but buyers cannot verify it before purchase. What market friction is present?
An economist observes that a borrower knows more about the riskiness of a project than the lender. Why can exchange be inefficient?
keys: Unobserved borrower risk can distort loan pricing and credit allocation

groups.stem: Consider a case in which both sides can cheaply verify quality and actions. What happens to the information-asymmetry problem?
Suppose that a platform publishes independently verified quality histories. What is the likely mechanism?
keys: Better information can support mutually beneficial trades

groups.stem: Suppose that people expecting high medical costs are especially likely to buy generous insurance before coverage begins. What problem appears?
An economist observes that buyers cannot distinguish reliable used products from defective ones, so they offer only an average price. What can follow?
keys: High-quality sellers may exit, lowering average quality

groups.stem: Suppose that a warranty is purchased disproportionately by customers who privately know their devices are fragile. Which timing identifies the issue?
keys: Hidden type affects contracting before covered behavior occurs

groups.stem: An economist observes that a bank expects a guaranteed bailout and therefore chooses a riskier portfolio. What causes the distortion?
keys: Protection shifts part of the downside to others

groups.stem: Suppose that behavior is perfectly monitored and a contract can condition payment on every action. What happens to hidden-action moral hazard?
keys: It can be greatly reduced through enforceable incentives

groups.stem: An economist observes that an insurer offers a high-deductible and a low-deductible plan so customers reveal risk through their choice. What mechanism is this?
Suppose that a lender requires collateral before approving a loan. What informational role can collateral play?
keys: It screens or separates borrowers by willingness and ability to bear default consequences
It can screen or separate borrowers by the consequences they accept if they default

groups.stem: An economist observes that a default enrollment rule sharply changes participation even though opting out is easy. What does this challenge?
keys: The claim that only final prices and outcomes matter, not choice architecture

groups.stem: Suppose that a behavior appears in one small sample. What is the strongest scientific response?
keys: Seek replication and compare predictive performance against alternative models

groups.stem: An economist observes that a person weighs a $100 loss more heavily than an equal-sized $100 gain. Which pattern fits?
Suppose that a dramatic recent news story leads residents to overestimate a rare risk. Which heuristic fits?
An economist observes that adding an irrelevant losing option reverses society's ranking of two unchanged alternatives. Which Arrow condition is implicated?
An economist observes that pairwise social preferences are A>B, B>C, and C>A. What is this called?
Suppose that voters have single-peaked preferences over one tax-rate line and choose by majority rule. Which position is pivotal?
